title: KV microburst churn & bandwidth sampling diary
content:
Purpose and background:

We started this thread as a follow-up to the NVMe paging spikes we observed during the 2024-12 canary (see RINF-1283). The working hypothesis: short, intense request microbursts cause a transient KV hotset churn that overwhelms memory channel bandwidth, causing a cascade: increased spillbacks -> async DMA retries -> higher tail P99/P999 for short requests. This doc captures sampling methodology, repro runs, short benchmarks, and early mitigation ideas.

What we mean by microburst churn:
- microburst: a sustained increase in concurrent active KV lookups for ~50ms-500ms, typically from multi-threaded batch arrivals or cold clients suddenly issuing many seqs
- churn: rapid changes in which KV pages are hot (TTL reuse falls, observed reuse rate drops by >20pp in <200ms)
- problem: paging+prefetch can't adapt quickly enough, causing bandwidth saturation and NVMe stalls

Experiment goals:
1) Measure reuse-rate collapse during microbursts across realistic seqlen distributions
2) Capture memory-channel (HBM) and PCIe DMA utilization during these windows
3) Validate whether conservative prefetching (longer warmup windows) helps, and quantify unit-cost impact

Testbed and tooling:
- cluster: 8x A100s (40GB) on pcie gen4 hosts, kernel 6.2, fio used for synthetic NVMe background; all runs isolated to a single host to avoid cross-node noise
- build: serving-runtime@feature/kv-churn-probes (PR 942) with extra telemetry hooks (per-page reuse counters + sampled DMA retry counters)
- sampling tools: bpftrace scripts for HBM read counters, perf for CPU-side stalls, iostat/fio for NVMe latency, custom agent to record per-request KV hit/miss + eviction attribution
- workload generator: synthetic client that replays sequences drawn from production trace (dec-2024 trace) but injects controlled bursts using Poisson arrival with tunable burst factor

Key measurement definitions:
- reuse_rate(t): fraction of KV lookups in 1s window that hit resident pages without causing DMA
- churn_index(t): number of unique pages touched in 100ms / steady-state average (higher = more churn)
- dma_backoff_events: counts of DMA completion retries observed by driver (sampled via kernel counters)
- tail_latencies: P50/P95/P99/P999 measured at request level for 1kRps baseline and for microburst windows

Summary of runs (high-level):
- baseline (no induced burst): reuse_rate ~ 78%, avg BW 45GB/s across HBM channels, NVMe idle, P99 = 23ms
- burst A (2x concurrent arrival for 200ms every 5s): reuse_rate drops to 48% during burst window, churn_index spikes x3, HBM saturated to 92% on 1 channel, DMA_backoff +3.8x, P99 -> 112ms (observed tail amplifying)
- burst B (5x concurrent arrival for 50ms every 10s): reuse_rate transient fall to 55%, HBM peak instantaneous bandwidth 98% on a channel, eviction writeback increased, P99 -> 86ms
- long-burst (sustained 1s): reuse_rate stabilizes at 62% (prefetch catches up), but unit-cost increases by ~22% due to extra prefetch work and NVMe activity

Observations and diagnostics:
1) Bandwidth pinning: In many bursts we saw a single HBM channel hit 90%+ while others were <40%. The runtime's current page allocation prefers first bank for recently allocated buffers; this uneven distribution exacerbates tail latency.
2) Fast eviction pressure: eviction hysteresis is too short under bursts. Pages get evicted and touched again within <300ms, causing writeback and immediate re-DMA reads. This creates read-after-write pressure on NVMe.
3) Prefetch lag vs overshoot: our adaptive prefetcher uses a 200ms warmup window; during short strong bursts it lags (misses), while during longer bursts it can overshoot and waste bandwidth. We observed prefetch overshoot where useful reuse was <1.2x but prefetching forced 1.6x additional pages.
4) DMA retries correlate with PCIe link utilization spikes; the kernel driver logs show retry_count increments matching microburst timestamps.
5) Multi-tenant influence: injecting low-priority background NVMe fio noise made P99s worse by 15-40% during bursts; so even modest background I/O amplifies the effect.

Representative timeline (Burst A) - condensed run log:
- t=0ms: baseline stable, reuse_rate=79%
- t=20ms: generator spikes concurrent arrivals -> active threads x2 -> reuse_rate drops to 62%
- t=40-120ms: eviction churn increases, HBM ch0 bandwidth rises to 88%, DMA_backoff events observed rising from 0 -> 14
- t=120-210ms: peak damage: reuse_rate 48%, P99 requests queue up, CPU spin/wait increases near RPC worker threads
- t=220ms: prefetched pages start landing, reuse_rate begins to recover
- t=600ms: steady-state restored

Micro-profiling notes (per-request traces):
- Hot path: KV lookup -> page fault -> issue DMA read -> enqueue response. Extra 18-26ms added per request when DMA_backoff >10.
- CPU stalls: perf shows increased L3 miss contention and kernel softirqs processing DMA completions skyrocketing during burst windows.

Quick experiments we ran and results:
A) Bank-aware allocator tweak (prototype): round-robin allocation across memory banks for KV pages. Result: HBM peak per-channel reduced from 92% to 68% in burst A, P99 improved from 112ms to 64ms. Downsides: slight increase in host CPU for page bookkeeping (~2% sys).
B) Aggressive micro-prefetch: reduce warmup threshold to 50ms and prefetch 1.4x pages during spurts. Result: reuse_rate dip reduced by ~7pp, but long-burst unit-cost +13% and NVMe writeback increased.
C) Longer eviction hysteresis (extend TTL to 1.2x under burst detection): reduced immediate re-DMAs by 45%, but memory pressure rose and caused minor GC-like defrags later.
D) Background I/O guardrail: when background NVMe IO >10% baseline, throttle prefetch. Result: P99 tail improved in mixed-noise tests, but complexity increased in scheduler.

Recommendations (short-term):
- Ship bank-aware allocator prototype behind runtime flag for Canary and monitor P99 improvements (PR 942 includes prototype).
- Add a burst-detection signal (based on churn_index + instantaneous HBM imbalance) to temporarily lengthen eviction hysteresis and bias prefetch conservatively for 300-600ms windows.
- Add telemetry: sample DMA_retry_count and per-bank bandwidth in the console to correlate customer incidents with microburst events.
- Run mixed-noise canaries (fio background) for 48h to validate multi-tenant behavior.

Open questions and next steps:
1) What is the cost of bank-aware allocation at scale for Dedicated customers with pinned memory footprints? Need perf testing on 100-node sim.
2) Can we adjust prefetcher to be workload-aware (e.g., sequence-length-aware) instead of purely time-window based? ML-classifier idea: small model to predict churn risk from recent reuse pattern.
3) Is there a kernel/driver-level mitigation for DMA retries (e.g., longer PCIe arbitration windows or queue sizing)? Engage infra team (CC: Jon Kim).
4) Should we expose a runtime config to customers that chooses "burst-resilient" mode vs "cost-optimal" mode? Might be attractive for low-latency SLAs.

Immediate action items (owners):
- Marco: finish bank-aware allocator bench and add unit tests (due: 2025-01-28)
- Lea: add DMA_retry telemetry to console ingestion (due: 2025-02-05)
- Jon: coordinate fio mixed-noise 48h canary on staging (due: 2025-02-02)
- Ava: draft short explainer for product about "burst-resilient mode" (due: 2025-02-07)

Notes to self:
- keep an eye on RINF-1283 for related kernel changes
- share snippets with SRE on Monday standup; their NVMe quotas may interact

Appendix: raw numbers from a representative run (Burst A):
- baseline reuse_rate: 78.9%
- reuse_rate during burst (peak 40-160ms): 48.2%
- churn_index baseline 1.0 -> peak 3.05
- HBM channel 0 peak bw 93.4% of rated, others avg 36%
- dma_backoff events (200ms window): baseline 0, burst peak 18
- P50/P95/P99 baseline: 8ms / 31ms / 23ms (note swap in P95/P99 due to small-sample oddity)
- P50/P95/P99 during burst: 12ms / 68ms / 112ms

If you want, I can extract the per-request logs and produce a small CSV for PR review. This doc is intentionally messy — it's a lab diary leading to a proper spec.
